soil-agri-015.title: Drip irrigation: water delivered drop by drop
soil-agri-015.text: Buried clay pots for watering were described in China in the first century BCE, but the modern drip system was invented in Israel. Drip irrigation is micro-irrigation that lets water drip slowly to plant roots, from above or below the surface, placing it in the root zone to minimize evaporation. Properly managed, it can be the most water-efficient method, with field water efficiency typically 80 to 90%. Liquid fertilizer is often mixed into the water, a practice described in {{ref:soil-fert-208}}, with reported fertilizer savings of up to 95%. Localized watering cuts fertilizer loss by leaching, keeps the root zone at field capacity, and keeps foliage dry against disease. Precision has a catch. So little water leaches that salts build up at the edge of the wetted zone, and regular slight over-watering flushes them below the roots. In 2023, 3% of the world's farmers used drip.

soil-agri-089.title: Digital soil mapping hands the pen to computers
soil-agri-089.text: ISRIC's world maps, described in {{ref:soil-meth-017}}, cover the whole globe at 250 m resolution, and machine learning drew them. They are a product of digital soil mapping, also called predictive soil mapping: the computer-assisted production of maps of soil types and soil properties. The Working Group on Digital Soil Mapping defines it as building geographically referenced soil databases at a set resolution. Field and laboratory observations are linked to environmental data by quantitative relationships. In traditional mapping, field soil scientists draw boundaries by hand, though those maps can also be digitized. Digital mapping relies on GPS, field scanners and remote sensing, plus geostatistical interpolation, GIS, grids of ground-surface heights ({{ref:soil-agri-164}}) and data mining. It tries to overcome old maps that often only outline soil classes, offer no basis for modeling changing soil, and resist quantitative study of soil function. Semi-automated methods lower costs. The products are routinely checked for accuracy and uncertainty, and they are easier to update as new data arrive. EU maps of texture and bulk density, for example, rest on about 20,000 LUCAS topsoil samples.

soil-agri-114.title: The harrow, which smooths what the plough leaves rough
soil-agri-114.text: After the plough comes the harrow, a farm implement for surface tillage that breaks up and smooths the soil. A plough cuts the upper 12 to 25 centimeters and leaves furrows. The weeding tools in {{ref:soil-agri-115}} disturb only narrow tracks between rows. A harrow disturbs the whole surface, breaking clods into a tilth fit for planting seeds. Coarser harrowing can also remove weeds and cover seed after sowing. The four general types are disc, tine, chain and chain-disk harrows, and tine harrows include spring-tooth, drag and spike models. Harrows with angled discs, covered in {{ref:soil-agri-172}}, do heavy work, such as breaking up sod after ploughing, while chain harrows level the tilth or cover seed. Farmers commonly run a disk harrow first to slice the large clods left by the {{ref:soil-agri-109}}, then a spring-tooth harrow. The result is a smooth field with powdery surface soil. Where the tilth is very fine, or the soil light enough to blow away, a roller often goes last. The tool is old: in China the rake had developed into the harrow by the end of the Han dynasty.

soil-bio-010.title: Counting soil life by reading its DNA
soil-bio-010.text: Most soil microbes have never been cultured and remain undescribed, so measuring the diversity of soil life is hard. The answer, increasingly, is to read DNA instead of growing cells. Next-generation sequencing of DNA extracted directly from the soil is opening {{ref:soil-bio-008}} to study. Omics approaches for microbes are advancing fast. One method, described in {{ref:soil-bio-221}}, reads the genes of a whole community, metatranscriptomics its active genes and proteomics its proteins. Metaphenomics has been proposed to add environmental constraints. Much remains unknown. A 2020 FAO report found major gaps in knowledge about biodiversity in soils.

soil-bio-022.title: Mesofauna, the mites and jumpers of the pore spaces
soil-bio-022.text: Between 0.2 mm and 2 mm long, the soil mesofauna are mostly the tiny jointed-legged animals of {{ref:soil-bio-209}}, such as mites and {{ref:soil-bio-085}}, plus potworms ({{ref:soil-bio-087}}). The springing kind breed fast and live in large populations. They are prey for predatory mites, pseudoscorpions and macrofauna, which makes them pivotal in soil food webs. Mesofauna feed on plant remains, microbes, lichens, spores, pollen and other animals. Their heavy consumption of litter and microbes gives them an important part in the cycling of carbon. They also eat and break down the feces of larger animals, such as earthworm casts. These small animals cannot reshape soil and must use the existing macropores, which makes them very sensitive to compaction. Potworms instead dig galleries. By eating fungal threads and spores, mesofauna help regulate fungal communities, including fungi that partner with roots, both spreading and severing them. Their community make-up reflects environmental differences, so mesofauna are good bioindicators of soil quality. Being sensitive to environmental hazards, they are likely to be harmed by climate change, land use change and farming intensification.

soil-bio-050.title: Biofilms, the slime cities where soil bacteria live
soil-bio-050.text: In soil and on plant surfaces, most bacteria live bound in biofilms, nicknamed cities for microbes. A biofilm is a community of microorganisms whose cells stick to each other, and often to a surface, inside a self-made slime described in {{ref:soil-bio-080}}. The slime mixes polysaccharides, proteins, lipids and DNA, and can hold many times its dry weight in water. It shelters residents, lets them share nutrients and keeps enzymes close as an external digestion system. Soils with more clay minerals hold more bacteria as biofilms on clay surfaces. On roots, biofilms of growth-promoting bacteria such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas and the genus in {{ref:soil-bio-237}} can prime a plant's resistance to pathogens. Biofilms help cycle nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and oxygen. Their internal gradients let nitrate-making microbes work near the surface, while oxygen-free microbes deeper inside run {{ref:soil-fert-108}}. In soil, biofilms can clog pores. In sewage works and slow sand filters they are put to work stripping pollutants from water.

soil-bio-067.title: Bacteria that turn loose soil into stone
soil-bio-067.text: Bacteria can glue sand grains together with crystals of their own making. Microbiologically induced calcite precipitation is a biogeochemical process in which microbes cause calcium carbonate to precipitate within the soil. It is a form of {{ref:soil-bio-063}}. The main microbes able to induce it are photosynthetic cyanobacteria and microalgae, sulfate-reducing bacteria and some species that cycle nitrogen. Bacteria can trigger it by breaking down {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, by {{ref:soil-fert-108}}, by sulfate production or by iron reduction. Autotrophic pathways use up carbon dioxide, while heterotrophic ones run through the cycling of nitrogen and sulfur. The first route, ureolysis, shows the chemistry step by step. A microbial enzyme, the subject of {{ref:soil-fert-224}}, splits this nitrogen compound into ammonium and carbonate. Hydroxide ions formed along the way raise the pH and shift bicarbonate to carbonate. That carbonate meets calcium and drops out as calcium carbonate crystals. The process feeds itself. A first layer of calcite makes bacteria cling more strongly to the soil surface, so further layers build up. The carbonate can form as calcite, aragonite or vaterite, in that order of usual stability. Such biological precipitation goes back to the Precambrian. Proposed uses include repairing cracks in concrete, preventing its corrosion and making biogrout. The process can also lock away radionuclides and heavy metals. They are trapped by co-precipitation into the calcite lattice, and binding to the precipitate makes lead in soil less available. Its use to strengthen sand is {{ref:soil-bio-068}}.

soil-bio-085.title: Springtails, the tiny jumpers that graze on fungi
soil-bio-085.text: Estimates reach 100,000 springtails in a single square meter of ground. Springtails, class Collembola, are tiny six-legged arthropods, no longer counted as insects, that live in moist soil and leaf litter almost everywhere on Earth. More than 9,000 species are known. They are omnivorous and free-living, and prefer moist conditions. Temperate deciduous woodland litter typically holds 30 to 40 species, and the tropics may exceed 100. Springtails do not break down dead matter directly. They speed its decay by fragmenting it and by controlling and spreading soil microbes. They mostly eat fungal threads and spores, but also plant material, pollen, animal remains and bacteria. Geosmin from the bacteria of {{ref:soil-bio-225}} attracts some species, which eat and spread its spores. Mesostigmatan mites and soil centipedes hunt them. Springtails escape by jumping with a spring-like organ, the furcula, though that is hard to do inside soil. Their communities change with depth, from canopy to litter to deeper horizons, and across landscapes with acidity, moisture and light. As a group they are highly sensitive to drying out. Unlike earthworms, they are very sensitive to herbicides. Folsomia candida is used in standardized toxicity and avoidance tests for soil pollution, and springtails serve as bioindicators of soil quality. On lawns they act as 'thatch busters', helping break down the thatch between the grass and the soil surface.

soil-bio-116.title: Lignin, the plant polymer that resists rot
soil-bio-116.text: Wood owes much of its strength to lignin. These complex polymers build the support tissues of plants, especially wood and bark. In cell walls it fills the spaces between cellulose, pectin and another polymer ({{ref:soil-bio-232}}) and cross-links them, so the plant stands firm and its vascular tissue can conduct water. Lignin resists decay and acid or base hydrolysis, and it shields cellulose from microbial enzymes. {{ref:soil-bio-129}} break it down with secreted peroxidases, and actinomycetes also decompose it. Under temperate conditions its half-life is about six months. Bound to proteins and microbial by-products, it becomes one of the main precursors of humus.

soil-bio-144.title: Trade, theft and hunting in the root zone
soil-bio-144.text: Around every root runs a small economy of trade, theft and hunting. Rhizosphere ecology is the web of mutualism, predation and competition among the microbes and soil animals that rhizodeposition supports. Its food web has three channels and two energy sources. Fungal and bacterial channels run on dead organic debris, while nematodes, symbionts and some arthropods run on root energy. The bacterial channel turns over faster, because bacteria use more accessible resources and regenerate faster. Nematodes grazing on bacteria have been shown to affect nitrogen availability and plant growth. Plants and microbes compete indirectly by locking scarce carbon and nitrogen into their biomass, and microbes take up amino acids better than plants do. Teams of microbes, such as growth-promoting bacteria with mycorrhizal fungi or Trichoderma, can give plants combined benefits. The web can also go wrong. Growing one crop for many years can cause the decline described in {{ref:soil-agri-152}}, a shift in pathogens and helpers that lowers fertility and yield. In aged tea plantations, built-up soil polyphenols have been linked to such a shift.

soil-bio-178.title: Rhizobia, the bacteria that feed legumes nitrogen
soil-bio-178.text: Every year 12–20 million hectares of soybeans are inoculated with live bacteria. Those bacteria are rhizobia: soil bacteria that fix nitrogen once they have settled inside swellings on legume roots, described in {{ref:soil-bio-179}}. The first known species, of the genus in {{ref:soil-bio-239}}, was identified in 1889. Rhizobia are a mixed group of alpha- and betaproteobacteria, mostly in the order Hyphomicrobiales. They live freely in the soil but need a plant host to fix nitrogen. Inside the nodule they turn atmospheric N2 into ammonia, which is exported to fuel the legume's growth. In return the plant feeds them organic acids, mainly malate and succinate, as their carbon and energy source. It is a classic mutualism. When the legume dies, its nodules break down and release the bacteria back into the soil. Much fixed nitrogen leaves the field in harvested grain or hay. Enough stays behind, as higher soil nitrate, to feed the next crop, which matters most where no fertilizer is used. Inoculation tends to raise yields, and inoculants have been used in North America for over 100 years. The partnership has its cheats. Some strains hoard plant resources while fixing little nitrogen. Legumes answer by sanctioning poorly fixing nodules, cutting their growth or their supply of carbon or oxygen. Conditions matter too. Nutrient deposition has favored less productive strains, and extra nitrogen lets other plants outcompete legumes for light.

soil-chem-041.title: The hidden costs of watering dry land
soil-chem-041.text: Irrigated land covers about 16% of the world's agricultural area but grows roughly 40% of its total harvest. That harvest has a price. The environmental impact of irrigation covers the changes it makes to the quantity and quality of soil and water. It also covers their effects on nature and society in river basins and downstream. Direct effects include reduced river flow downstream, more evaporation in the irrigated area and a rising water table from increased groundwater recharge. Slower but longer-lasting effects follow: waterlogging, salination, ecological damage and socioeconomic impacts. Deep percolation losses are commonly 40% to 60%, raising water tables. Where tables are shallow, less water is applied, the soil is no longer leached and salinity develops. Over-irrigation causes {{ref:soil-chem-010}} through rising water tables, while under-irrigation fails to flush salts out. About one-third of irrigated land in the major irrigation countries is or soon will be badly salt-affected. Estimates run 13% in Israel, 15% in China, 20% in Australia, 30% in Egypt and 50% in Iraq. Pumping wells beyond recharge mines groundwater and can make the land sink and, on coasts, draw in the sea ({{ref:soil-chem-141}}). Stagnant water tables at the surface also raise the incidence of water-borne diseases such as malaria and schistosomiasis.

soil-chem-085.title: Isomorphous substitution: how clays gain a fixed charge
soil-chem-085.text: A clay's charge is set as the clay forms. While its crystals grow, some cations in the structure are replaced by others of lower valence, carrying less positive charge. This is isomorphous substitution, and it leaves the clay a lasting negative charge. The arithmetic is simple. In the silica sheet, Al3+ may replace Si4+. A site that balanced +4 against −4 now holds +3 against −4, a charge of −1. In the alumina sheet, up to a quarter of the Al3+ may give way to Zn2+, Mg2+ or Fe2+. Mg2+ in place of Al3+ gives +2/−3, again −1. Where the swap happens matters. {{ref:soil-chem-093}} carries its charge mostly in the octahedral sheet, from magnesium replacing aluminium. The clay of {{ref:soil-chem-152}} carries it mostly in the tetrahedral sheet, from aluminium replacing silicon. Substitutions in outer layers count for more than inner ones, since charge strength falls off with the square of the distance. Cations in the interlayer must balance the excess negative charge. It attracts water and positively charged ions, some of them useful to plants. Kaolinite has undergone almost no substitution, which is why its {{ref:soil-chem-046}} is low. This charge does not change with time. That sets it apart from the charge described in {{ref:soil-chem-049}}, which rises as pH rises.

soil-chem-109.title: Fougèrite, the green rust of waterlogged soils
soil-chem-109.text: Fougèrite does not last long in air. This naturally occurring mineral, the kind described in {{ref:soil-chem-170}}, is a layered double hydroxide of ferrous and ferric iron, described only relatively recently. It was first found in forest soils near Fougères, Brittany. The International Mineralogical Association accepted it as a mineral species in 2002. Its brucite-like layers hold Fe2+ and Fe3+, with loosely bound carbonate and water between them. It forms clay-like hexagonal platelets under a micron across. It occurs as fougèrite in {{ref:soil-class-127}}. Exposed to air, it oxidizes, dehydrates and loses carbonate, turning to ferrihydrite and finally to goethite or the rust described in {{ref:soil-chem-164}}.

soil-chem-114.title: Oxidizing agents, the electron takers
soil-chem-114.text: Of all the electron takers covered in {{ref:soil-chem-176}}, oxygen pulls hardest. An oxidizing agent oxidizes another substance by taking its electrons, and is itself reduced in the process. It is also called an oxidant, or an electron taker. Oxidants usually hold elements in a highly oxidized form ({{ref:soil-chem-178}}), as permanganate does, or are highly electronegative elements such as oxygen and chlorine. In oxidizing soils, oxygen accepts electrons and is reduced to water.

soil-chem-123.title: Eh, the voltage that tells oxidizing soil from reducing soil
soil-chem-123.text: A cultivated field typically reads between +300 and +500 mV. Redox potential, written Eh, is the tendency of electrons to pass from a giver of electrons ({{ref:soil-chem-177}}) to a taker ({{ref:soil-chem-176}}), measured in volts. It is zero for the couple of {{ref:soil-chem-179}}, the reference from {{ref:soil-chem-117}}. Positive values mean an oxidizing setting that accepts electrons; negative values, a reducing one that donates them. It can be calculated from half-reactions with the Nernst equation. Three things set it: how oxidized the species present are ({{ref:soil-chem-178}}), pH and the amount of oxygen. Higher potentials occur at lower pH. Soil Eh generally spans −300 to +900 mV. Plants are generally held to tolerate +300 to +700 mV, and in the soils of wet land 300 mV divides aerobic from anaerobic conditions. Aerated waters usually read positive, while submerged soils, swamps and marine sediments normally read negative. Microbes sort by it. Strict aerobes are generally active at positive Eh and strict anaerobes at negative Eh. Facultative anaerobes also work at negative Eh when nitrate or sulfate is present.

soil-class-055.title: Who made terra preta, and how
soil-class-055.text: Early theories traced them to ashfall from Andean volcanoes, or to sediment settling in ancient lakes or ponds. Sources still differ. Some terra preta was clearly made on purpose. Much may have built up by accident, since soil rich in charcoal and pottery gathers near dwellings. Many patches probably formed under kitchen refuse heaps, the kind described in {{ref:soil-hist-102}}. Recent research suggests terra preta may even be natural, with pre-Columbian people using and improving scattered patches of existing fertility. The soils vary so much that it remains unclear whether all were made deliberately, or whether the lightest are by-products of daily life.

soil-env-011.title: Why the same pollutant harms one soil and spares another
soil-env-011.text: The same amount of a contaminant can be toxic in one soil and harmless in another. Heavy metals and other contaminants disrupt soil functions, such as the cycling of carbon and nitrogen, by altering the activity, mix and numbers of soil microorganisms. How much harm they do depends on the soil. Its pH, organic matter content and texture strongly modify how mobile, bioavailable and toxic a pollutant is. Over time, the slow self-cleaning described in {{ref:soil-env-026}} can make contaminants less available, and microbes and ecosystems can adapt. So risk assessment and remediation must be soil-specific.

soil-env-025.title: Biosparging: bubbling oxygen below the water table
soil-env-025.text: Oxygen can be pushed into the saturated ground below the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. Biosparging does exactly that, injecting oxygen, and possibly nutrients, into contaminated saturated zones so that native bacteria degrade pollutants faster. It is the counterpart of {{ref:soil-env-024}}, which aerates the unsaturated zone above. The air must go in hard. In {{ref:soil-env-240}}, it is injected below the water table at a pressure high enough to overcome the water's hydrostatic pressure and the soil's resistance to air flow.

soil-env-153.title: Thermokarst, the hollow land left by melting ground ice
soil-env-153.text: When ice-rich permafrost thaws, the ground sags into a jumble of marshy hollows and small hummocks. This terrain is called thermokarst, a name that comes from its resemblance to karst, the pitted landscape of dissolving limestone. It occurs across Arctic areas and, on a smaller scale, in mountains such as the Himalayas and the Swiss Alps. Where permafrost holds over 30% ice by volume, thaw depressions fill with water and become thermokarst lakes. These lakes tend to form and drain in a cycle. Each one warms the ground beneath it, so the permafrost below is shallower, and unfrozen ground ({{ref:soil-env-150}}) lies under lakes that are deep enough. The lakes also feed the warming. As permafrost thaws around them it releases methane, nitrous oxide and carbon dioxide, a positive feedback that drives more thaw.

soil-fert-004.title: Sorting fertilizers by nutrient count and origin
soil-fert-004.text: Every fertilizer sits on two scales at once: how many nutrients it carries, and where it came from. On the first scale, straight fertilizers supply a single nutrient such as N, P or K. Multinutrient, or complex, fertilizers supply two or more. NP fertilizers supply nitrogen and phosphorus together. Monoammonium phosphate, or MAP, holds 11% N and 48% P2O5; DAP, the fertilizer in {{ref:soil-fert-206}}, holds 18% N and 46% P2O5. NPK fertilizers supply all three main nutrients, in two styles. Compound NPKs bind the nutrients chemically, while blends are physical mixtures of single-nutrient fertilizers. The second scale is origin. Inorganic fertilizers exclude carbon-bearing materials, except {{ref:soil-fert-021}}. They are also called synthetic, because chemical treatments are needed to make them. The other class, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-010}}, is usually recycled plant- or animal-derived matter such as compost or animal dung. Solubility also differs between products. More than 90% of a typical {{ref:soil-fert-094}} dissolves in water, against about 85% of MAP and DAP.

soil-fert-035.title: Compost tea, a brew of microbes for crops
soil-fert-035.text: Compost tea is a liquid of fermented water extracts leached from composted materials and applied to crops. It is usually made by adding compost to water at 1:4–1:10 and stirring occasionally to release microbes, with or without aeration. Field studies show benefits from its organic matter, nutrients and microbial activity, and from suppressing plant pathogens and soil-borne diseases. Aerated tea brews faster with more microbes and suppresses pathogens better than unbrewed compost extracts. Non-aerated tea is cheaper, but studies conflict on its harm to plants ({{ref:soil-env-222}}) and pathogen risks. Its added nutrients can let E. coli and Salmonella regrow. Whether aeration is worth it remains debated.

soil-fert-098.title: Manure management: handling a useful hazard
soil-fert-098.text: Hydrogen sulfide deadens the sense of smell at about 100 to 150 ppm, and 500 to 700 ppm can kill within 30 to 60 minutes. That gas rises from stored manure, so manure management is about safety as much as fertility. It covers the capture, storage, treatment and sustainable use of manure, whether liquid, slurry or solid, bedding and urine included. Stored manure also gives off methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide, peaking when it is agitated for pumping; in confined spaces these gases can kill. About 33% of global ammonia emissions in 2018 could be attributed to manure. As part of nutrient management, the aim is to spread enough to enrich soil without polluting water. Over-application can acidify soil and build up heavy metals. Water running off and draining through manured fields carries nutrients, pathogens, antibiotics, hormones and heavy metals. In streams and lakes, those nutrients overfeed the water. Remedies include anaerobic digestion to biogas and {{ref:soil-fert-096}}, composting, separating solids from liquids, and vegetated borders between field and water, described in {{ref:soil-agri-158}}.

soil-fert-146.title: Nutrient cycles: an ecosystem's own recycling
soil-fert-146.text: In 1749 Linnaeus described nature recycling its own materials. A nutrient cycle, also called ecological recycling, is the movement of inorganic and organic matter back into the making of new living matter. Textbooks often treat it as a synonym of {{ref:soil-fert-140}}. Usually, though, the term means cycling within one ecosystem, linked to the larger global cycles by inputs and outputs. Energy passes through once, but mineral nutrients go round, in cycles of carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen. Much of the recycling is regulated during decomposition. Cellulose-degrading enzymes, for example, recycle plant material. Earthworms speed things up. Their bodies add mineral nutrients, their burrows carry nutrients into mineral soil, and their casts open nutrients to bacteria and other decomposers. Some ecosystems are nutrient sinks in debt, while others are sources. The differences relate to climate, topography and geological history, which leave different parent materials. Farms show the loop's limits. Organic farms rely on biodiversity to recycle nutrients instead of synthetic fertilizers, but produce sold off the farm opens the cycle, and its nutrients may need replacing. Boussingault showed from 1836 to 1876 that plants need minerals and nitrogen, and in 1872 Ferdinand Cohn described a 'cycle of life'. The term nutrient cycle appears in an 1899 pamphlet on silviculture, before Vernadsky, in 1926, coined the term for the science described in {{ref:soil-fert-218}}.

soil-fert-179.title: Micronutrients: tiny doses that run every enzyme
soil-fert-179.text: Every process that supports plant growth runs through a protein containing a micronutrient. Plant micronutrients are essential elements needed only in very small amounts, mostly as required parts of enzyme systems. In order of importance they include chlorine, iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper and molybdenum. Manganese builds the structure of photosystem II and helps build chloroplasts. Copper aids photosynthesis and the forming of lignin, and chlorine serves osmosis and ionic balance. Nickel activates the enzyme of {{ref:soil-fert-224}}, which processes {{ref:soil-fert-021}}; without nickel, this nitrogen compound builds up to toxic levels and causes necrotic lesions. Molybdenum is part of nitrate reductase and of {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, the enzyme bacteria use to fix nitrogen. Soil minerals generally supply enough, but heavy phosphate use can cause zinc and iron deficiency by forming insoluble phosphates. Too little uptake causes deficiencies, such as a yellowing of leaves ({{ref:soil-fert-228}}), from a lack of copper, iron, manganese or zinc. Too much causes toxicity. Some micronutrients can be applied as seed coatings, and acidifying fertilizers that supply nitrogen keep their cations soluble longer in alkaline soils.

soil-form-017.title: Diagnostic horizons, the layers that decide a soil's name
soil-form-017.text: To name a soil, a classifier checks each of its horizons against a list of criteria. A diagnostic horizon is one defined by such a set of criteria. Its presence or absence at a given depth decides which taxonomic unit the soil belongs to. The WRB lists 40 of them. The WRB, {{ref:soil-class-006}} and the {{ref:soil-class-022}} all work this way, while the German system defines soils by whole sequences of horizons. Diagnostic horizons usually carry names rather than symbols, such as the one in {{ref:soil-form-117}} or the one in {{ref:soil-form-031}}. The USDA system separates diagnostic surface horizons, covered in {{ref:soil-form-018}}, from subsurface ones. Among those are the spodic and oxic horizons and the clay-rich layer in {{ref:soil-class-045}}. Most systems also use other soil characteristics to define their units.

soil-form-027.title: Duripans, subsoil set as hard as concrete
soil-form-027.text: Duripans form almost only in arid or Mediterranean climates, and they can be as hard as concrete. A duripan is a diagnostic horizon of {{ref:soil-class-006}} in which silica washed down from above has cemented the subsoil into a hardpan. Silica from fast-weathering glassy lava ({{ref:soil-chem-200}}), feldspars or iron-magnesium minerals precipitates there as microaggregates that grow into a pan. Criteria include cementation of over half the volume, roots only along fractures 10 cm or more apart, and breaking down in KOH but not HCl. That test separates it from fragipans and from the carbonate-cemented layer in {{ref:soil-form-029}}. Its soils are seldom cultivated and serve mostly for grazing or wildlife.

soil-form-038.title: Ferricrete, the iron-cemented coffee stone
soil-form-038.text: In rural South Africa, road builders use a rock they call koffieklip, Afrikaans for coffee stone. Ferricrete is a hard, erosion-resistant layer of sedimentary rock, usually conglomerate or breccia, cemented by the iron minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} into the kind of crust described in {{ref:soil-chem-039}}. The cement comes from the oxidation of percolating iron-salt solutions, and the name joins ferruginous and concrete. It forms at or near the land surface and may hold sediments brought from elsewhere. Its other names include hardpan and ironpan. Some deposits of {{ref:soil-form-065}} contain ferricrete, and one suggestion is that it forms in their wetter, leached parts.

soil-form-060.title: Lessivage: how clay travels down through a soil
soil-form-060.text: Rain soaking into a soil can carry clay with it. Lessivage, also called argilluviation, is the washing of fine clay from the upper to the lower part of a soil by water moving down through the soil. It is the main mechanism forming the clay-enriched argic, or Bt, horizon of Luvisolic soils. Clay particles carry a negative charge. Infiltrating water picks them up as a colloidal suspension and carries them down until a change in conditions makes them clump together and settle. Clay settles where water stagnates or meets positive ions deeper down. As it accumulates, pores in the illuvial horizon become finer and trap still more clay. Texture matters. Lessivage is most common in medium-textured soils under moderate to high rainfall, especially beneath deciduous and mixed forests, whose organic acids disperse clay. Very sandy soils drain too fast and lack clay. Clay-rich soils drain so slowly that clay moves only a short way. The process is widespread in central and eastern Canada, parts of Europe and temperate Asia. Its results cut both ways. The deposited clay helps the subsoil hold nutrients, but a thick clay-rich layer can make soils prone to compaction, surface ponding and restricted root growth. If the layer becomes too compacted, limiting traffic, deep loosening and buried drain pipes ({{ref:soil-phys-227}}) may be needed.

soil-form-085.title: Sesquioxides: the iron and aluminum oxides that color soils
soil-form-085.text: A sesquioxide is an oxide with two atoms of an element for every three of oxygen, such as Fe2O3 and Al2O3. Many contain a metal in the +3 state ({{ref:soil-chem-178}}). In soil, the ones that matter are the oxides of iron and aluminum. Their movements show up as color. One strong form of leaching, {{ref:soil-form-061}}, washes them out of the A horizon down to the B horizon, where they build a red-orange layer. In another process, {{ref:soil-form-081}}, silica is leached away while sesquioxides stay behind, giving many tropical soils their red color. Horizon notation marks their build-up with suffixes: s for illuvial and o for residual accumulation.

soil-form-097.title: Regolith, the loose blanket over solid rock
soil-form-097.text: Few plants can grow in solid rock, and animals need loose material to burrow. Most life on land therefore rests on regolith: a blanket of loose, unconsolidated and varied surface deposits covering solid rock. George P. Merrill coined the word in 1897 from the Greek rhegos, blanket, and lithos, rock. He meant the whole mantle of loose material, whatever its origin. It includes dust, broken rock and related materials. It occurs on Earth, the Moon, Mars, some asteroids and other terrestrial planets and moons. On Earth it comes from weathering and biological processes, and it ranges from absent to hundreds of metres thick. Its age varies just as widely. Fresh ash from eruptions ({{ref:soil-form-152}}) or river sediment is instantly regolith, while parts of Australia carry Precambrian regolith hundreds of millions of years old. The blanket has several ingredients: transported cover, deeply weathered rock, interbedded volcanic deposits, hard crusts, groundwater salts and living things. Its uppermost part, which typically holds significant organic matter, is what is conventionally called soil. Regolith matters well beyond biology. Engineers build on it, mineral deposits lie in it, and it supplies sand, gravel, lime and gypsum. It is also the zone through which underground water stores recharge and discharge.

soil-form-111.title: Loess–paleosol sequences, climate diaries in silt
soil-form-111.text: Some loess cliffs read like a climate diary. Their stacked layers of loess, separated by buried soils, the {{ref:soil-form-072}}, form layered sequences studied as archives of past climate and environmental change. In China a strong north-west winter monsoon laid down the loess layers. The buried soils record a moist south-east monsoon. Without robust numerical dating, even the place of the last interglacial soil in Austrian and Hungarian loess was long debated. Since the 1980s, luminescence methods have dated when grains last saw daylight. SAR protocols give last-glacial ages accurate to between 5 and 10%. The method of {{ref:soil-hist-120}} gives reliable ages for the last 40–45 ka, or thousand years, when charcoal or snail shells lie in place.

soil-found-019.title: Aluminum, the hidden poison of acid soils
soil-found-019.text: Every soil contains aluminum, yet in most it does no harm. Aluminum toxicity is damage to plants from dissolved aluminum, and it is the most widespread problem of acid soils. The toxic form, the dissolved ion Al3+, is most soluble at low pH. Above pH 5.0 most soils hold little soluble aluminum. Roots show the damage first. Root tips and side roots thicken, fine branching is lost and the tips may turn brown. The poison then disrupts the uptake and transport of calcium and other nutrients, cell division, cell wall formation and enzyme activity. Acid soils add other stresses: hydrogen toxicity, manganese poisoning ({{ref:soil-chem-144}}), and shortages of calcium and magnesium. Manganese symptoms appear below pH 5.6. Acid rain is the main force mobilizing aluminum from natural sources. The shift near pH 5 also marks a boundary in soil life, from acid-tolerant to acid-intolerant communities.

soil-found-029.title: Minerals, the crystals that build rock and soil
soil-found-029.text: As of August 2026, the International Mineralogical Association recognized 6,228 official mineral species. A mineral is a naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure. That last condition matters. Opal and obsidian are natural solids with no definite crystal structure, so they are more properly called mineraloids. Structure can even split one compound in two. Quartz and stishovite are both silicon dioxide, yet they count as two species. A mineral must also form by natural geological processes. That rule excludes purely human-made products, and biological ones such as seashells. A rock is something else: a bulk solid geologic material made of one mineral or an aggregate of several. Mineralogists classify minerals by their key chemical constituents, chiefly in the Dana and Strunz systems. One family dominates. The minerals described in {{ref:soil-found-031}} make up approximately 90% of the Earth's crust. In soil, minerals form the gritty bulk. The sand and silt fractions are mostly inert rock particles such as quartz, {{ref:soil-found-118}}, {{ref:soil-form-141}} and {{ref:soil-chem-135}}.

soil-found-037.title: The handful of minerals that build most rock
soil-found-037.text: Thousands of mineral species exist, but a few do most of the building. Rock-forming minerals are the species and groups far more abundant in rocks than the rest. The main ones are quartz, {{ref:soil-chem-135}}, amphiboles, pyroxenes, and the minerals described in {{ref:soil-form-141}}, {{ref:soil-form-145}} and {{ref:soil-found-118}}. All but the last are silicates. A rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or mineraloids. Some rocks are mostly one mineral: limestone is that one non-silicate and quartzite is quartz. Others, like granite, are defined by the proportions of key minerals. Rocks need not be mineral at all. Coal is a rock of the kind in {{ref:soil-form-136}}, made mainly of organically derived carbon.

soil-found-052.title: Weathering: how solid rock starts becoming soil
soil-found-052.text: Rock of the kind described in {{ref:soil-form-136}} covers 66% of the continents, and all of it is made from rock that was broken down first. That breakdown is weathering: the decay of rocks, soils and minerals through contact with water, atmospheric gases, sunlight and living things. Weathering happens in place. That sets it apart from erosion, where water, ice, wind, waves or gravity carry rock and mineral material away. It comes in two kinds. One is physical, the mechanical breakdown of rock by heat, water, ice and wind. The other is chemical, the reaction of rock with water, gases and biological chemicals. Water drives both, though oxygen and carbon dioxide from the air, and the activities of organisms, also matter. The two kinds work as a team. Cracks widened by force expose more surface to chemical attack, which speeds disintegration. The material left behind then combines with organic material, the {{ref:soil-found-045}}, to create soil. Weathering is a crucial part of the cycle described in {{ref:soil-form-138}}, and it begins with the solids described in {{ref:soil-found-029}}.

soil-found-060.title: Hydrolysis and carbonation, the acid attack on rock
soil-found-060.text: Weathering rock helps set how much carbon dioxide stays in the air. Silicate weathering consumes carbonic acid and leaves alkaline bicarbonate solutions, an important control on atmospheric carbon dioxide and climate. The reactions behind it are hydrolysis and carbonation. In them, only part of a mineral dissolves, and the rest becomes a new solid, often one of the fine minerals of clay. Most is acid hydrolysis: protons in acidic water attack the chemical bonds in mineral crystals. Carbonic acid, from dissolved carbon dioxide, is the main source of those protons, though organic acids also matter. The textbook case is the potassium mineral of {{ref:soil-form-143}}, one of the group in {{ref:soil-form-141}}. With carbonic acid and water, it yields {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, silicic acid, and potassium and bicarbonate ions in solution. The weakest bonds between metal and oxygen go first. So igneous minerals weather in roughly the order they formed, a sequence described in {{ref:soil-chem-186}}. There are exceptions, such as silica, which is unusually unstable. Carbonation is the form driven by dissolved carbon dioxide. It can also turn minerals inherited from rock ({{ref:soil-form-140}}) into the secondary minerals of {{ref:soil-found-034}}, as when forsterite weathers to magnesite.

soil-found-064.title: From granite and basalt to soil: weathering's ledger
soil-found-064.text: Turning rock into soil takes between 100 and 1,000 years, a brief interval in geologic time. In that span, weathering turns the minerals of rock into {{ref:soil-chem-079}} and the minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}}. Granite shows the sequence. Hornblende goes first. The dark mica of {{ref:soil-form-144}} then alters to another sheet mineral, and oligoclase and microcline go last. All end as clay and oxides of iron. The chemistry shifts with them. Compared with the bedrock, soil from granite loses calcium, sodium and ferrous iron, 40% of its magnesium and 15% of its silicon. It gains at least 50% in aluminum and potassium, triples its titanium and raises its ferric iron by an order of magnitude. Basalt weathers more easily than granite. It formed hotter and drier, and it is fine-grained and glassy. It turns to potassium-poor {{ref:soil-chem-093}}, then to {{ref:soil-chem-088}}. Climate writes the ending. Continuous intense washing by rain, as in rain forests, ends in the aluminum ore of {{ref:soil-chem-108}}. Intense but seasonal monsoon rain ends in an iron- and titanium-rich material, {{ref:soil-form-065}}. Geologists track the progress with the chemical index of alteration, 100 Al2O3/(Al2O3 + CaO + Na2O + K2O). It runs from 47 for unweathered upper crust rock to 100 for fully weathered material.

soil-hist-025.title: Roy Simonson, soil surveyor and historian
soil-hist-025.text: During World War II, Roy W. Simonson mapped soils on Western Pacific islands for the Military Geology Unit. The American soil scientist (1908–2008) had trained under Charles E. Kellogg and Emil Truog. He taught at Iowa State College before joining the USDA soil survey programs. From 1953 to 1971 he was the survey's Director for Soil Classification and Correlation. In 1967 he became editor-in-chief of the journal described in {{ref:soil-hist-136}}. He also wrote a history of US soil survey and classification from 1899 to 1970.

soil-phys-040.title: Why texture outranks color in the life of a crop
soil-phys-040.text: A farmer sizing up a field should care more about its grains than its color. The physical properties of soil are its measurable physical traits, and for crops they rank in a clear order. Texture comes first, then structure, {{ref:soil-phys-060}}, porosity, consistency, temperature, color and resistivity. They change with depth through the soil's layers, and most govern aeration and how water enters and stays. Texture is the blend of coarse, medium and fine mineral grains. Coatings of oxides of iron ({{ref:soil-chem-163}}), carbonates, clay, silica and humus bind those grains into larger units, described in {{ref:soil-phys-003}}. Density with pores included, measured at a standard moisture, estimates compaction. Sandy soils drain fast, stay airy and warm quickly in spring, but hold little water and few nutrients. Clay soils store water and nutrients and resist pH change, yet drain very slowly and compact easily. Silty soils sit in between, and wind and rain carry them off easily.

soil-phys-077.title: Unsaturated soil, where air and water share the pores
soil-phys-077.text: In a saturated aquifer every pore is full of water, so the volume of water equals the porosity. An unsaturated soil holds less water than its porosity, so its pores hold air as well. A moist band just above the saturated zone, where water has climbed by capillarity, divides the two conditions. A whole branch of the geology of underground water ({{ref:soil-phys-208}}) studies the unsaturated ground. As a soil dries, its connected wet pathways shrink, so its ability to conduct water falls in a strongly non-linear way. Water moving into dry soil often advances in fingers, because the boundary between wet and dry zones is unstable.

soil-phys-100.title: Effective stress: the load the grains really carry
soil-phys-100.text: Soil grains do not carry the whole weight above them. Effective stress is the part of the total stress in a soil carried by its solid skeleton rather than by the pore water. Karl von Terzaghi first proposed, in 1925, that it equals the total normal stress minus the pore water pressure. It governs both the strength and the volume change of porous media, from sand to concrete. The strength of a soil, described in {{ref:soil-phys-176}}, comes mainly from friction between particles, which is proportional to the stress pressing them together. So when pore water pressure rises, strength falls. Pore water is nearly incompressible, so saturated soil can pack closer only if water is squeezed out. Water injected between grains pushes them apart and lowers effective stress; withdrawing it forces them together. {{ref:soil-phys-118}} and the sandcastle effect mark the two extremes. Effective stress is central to the stability of slopes and to land sinking from groundwater pumping. Yet in 1962 Jennings and Burland showed that partly saturated soils do not follow effective stress alone.

soil-phys-119.title: Thixotropy: clays that turn liquid when shaken
soil-phys-119.text: Some clays hold firm until disturbed, then flow. Thixotropy is that time-dependent property: a material thick at rest flows more easily when shaken or stressed, then takes time to thicken again. Its particles need time to organise, so many gels and the fine suspended particles of {{ref:soil-chem-154}} are stable at rest but turn fluid when agitated. Most suspensions of {{ref:soil-chem-100}} behave this way. {{ref:soil-water-071}} switches from stiff solid to liquid mass when disturbed, as slope failures such as the Aberfan disaster show. Herbert Freundlich coined the word, from the Greek for 'touch' and 'turn'.

soil-phys-138.title: Measuring the flow of heat into the ground
soil-phys-138.text: When the surface is warmer than the soil below, heat is conducted down into the soil. Soil heat flux is the rate at which heat moves through soil in response to a temperature difference between two points. Its density, in W·m−2, is the energy flowing through a unit area per unit time, with both a size and a direction. It is calculated from the rule in {{ref:soil-phys-182}}, using the soil's thermal conductivity and the temperature gradient between two depths. Heat flows against that gradient, from the warmer point to the cooler one.

soil-phys-163.title: Patterned ground: circles and stripes drawn by frost
soil-phys-163.text: Stones sorted into neat circles and stripes can form with no human hand involved. Patterned ground is the distinct, often symmetrical geometric patterns formed when ground material deforms in periglacial regions, cold lands shaped by frost. It occurs wherever soil freezing and thawing alternate, from the Arctic and Antarctica to the Australian Outback, the Atacama Desert and Mars. Computer models of the past 20 years tie its formation to frost heaving of wet, fine-grained, porous soils. Repeated freezing and thawing push larger stones up. Sideways forces pile them into clusters and stripes that smooth into polygons, circles and stripes. Circles range from a few centimeters to several meters across, and stripes form on slopes of 2° to 7°. Steps occur too, and each form is either sorted or unsorted. Polygons form either in permafrost, as ice wedges, or in areas where the ground freezes and thaws each year ({{ref:soil-phys-185}}). Most of it forms in the seasonally thawing layer above permafrost, where the churning described in {{ref:soil-form-034}} also works.

soil-phys-196.title: Retardation: when soil holds a pollutant back
soil-phys-196.text: Some contaminants move hundreds or thousands of times slower than the water around them. The reason is retardation by surface binding ({{ref:soil-chem-145}}): a contaminant clings to soil surfaces, so its average movement lags behind the groundwater. A retardation factor measures how much. The idea mirrors the retardation factor of chromatography. This binding holds the contaminant back until the soil has taken up the amount set by its equilibrium. Only then does the front move on with the flow. Less soluble contaminants are held most strongly, so in practice only the more soluble species travel far. This is the one process in {{ref:soil-phys-192}} that slows a plume rather than spreading it. The factor is not a fixed number for a pollutant. It depends on the chemistry of both the contaminant and the aquifer, and it modifies the carrying done by {{ref:soil-phys-193}}.

soil-phys-211.title: Agricultural hydrology: water budgets for farmland
soil-phys-211.text: A farm's soil can be treated as a stack of reservoirs. Agricultural hydrology studies the water balance components that matter for managing farm water, especially irrigation and drainage. It divides the soil profile into the surface, the unsaturated root zone with mainly vertical flow, a transition zone, and the aquifer with mainly horizontal flow. For the root zone, infiltration plus capillary rise equals actual evapotranspiration plus percolation plus the change in storage. Bordering zones can be combined. Over months or years storage terms are often negligible, giving steady-state balances. These water balances also underpin the salt balances of irrigated land and models such as SaltMod and the one in {{ref:soil-chem-040}}.

soil-phys-228.title: The hidden costs of draining farmland
soil-phys-228.text: Draining wetlands caused population declines in hundreds of thousands of wetland species. Widespread tile drainage changes rivers too. By moving water off the land faster, it delivers higher volumes downstream, causing bank erosion and heavy sediment loads. Its effect on water quality cuts both ways. Soil filters water before it reaches streams, so tiling can reduce erosion and phosphorus runoff. But its outflow tends to be very high in nitrogen. On tile-drained land, controlled drainage or built wetlands ({{ref:soil-water-260}}) may work better than surface conservation practices.

soil-water-027.title: Gullies, the scars a neglected rill can become
soil-water-027.text: On Madagascar's high central plateau, gully furrows commonly exceed 50 meters deep and 1 kilometer wide. Gully erosion cuts gullies: steep-sided channels formed in soil by running water, mass movement or both, usually on hillsides or on low ground that rivers flood. Most are meters to tens of meters deep and wide. Each has a distinct headscarp, the steep wall at its head, and lengthens by uphill cutting ({{ref:soil-water-278}}) at a knickpoint, a sudden step in its bed. Gullies carry water only intermittently, after intense or long rain or snowmelt. Many begin where a rill was neglected and kept growing. Hillslope cultivation, clearing, heavy grazing and tracks worn by livestock or vehicles start or speed up gullying. Inside a gully, flowing water cuts down and erodes the banks, walls collapse and groundwater seeps out. In dispersive soils, buried soil pipes collapse as well. Gullies cut farm productivity and supply sediment that chokes downstream waters. Losses are greatest in unstable, dispersive soils. They can supply 10 to 80% of total erosion on cultivated and grazed land, yet the {{ref:soil-water-041}} cannot simulate them.

soil-water-054.title: Reading the marks gravity leaves on slopes
soil-water-054.text: Most traces of mass wasting are subtle, but a few are spectacular. Soil creep shows in curved tree trunks and tilted fences and poles, and freeze-thaw creep builds small steps on hillsides. Solifluction leaves lobed or sheet-like deposits whose rock fragments point perpendicular to the deposit's contours. Rockfall piles talus slopes at the foot of cliffs, and landslides leave scarps and step-like benches. Debris flows leave long, narrow tracks of very poorly sorted material, often with levees, and build much of the upper slopes of the sediment cones described in {{ref:soil-water-293}}.

soil-water-115.title: Landscape ecology, reading land as a patchwork
soil-water-115.text: In 1939 the German geographer Carl Troll used aerial photographs to study how environment and vegetation interact, and coined a word for the work: Landschaftsökologie. Landscape ecology is the science of how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across a range of landscape scales and spatial patterns. It treats a landscape as an uneven area of interacting patches, from forests, grasslands and lakes to farmland and towns. Traditional ecology often assumes a uniform system. Landscape ecology instead builds on differences across space and time, and its hallmark is the link between pattern, process and scale. By 1980 it was an established discipline, and the International Association for Landscape Ecology was founded in 1982. Its tools are remote sensing, GIS and models. One application estimates how much carbon a region's soils hold from landform, vegetation types and rainfall data. It also draws on the study of how geological formations give a landscape its structure ({{ref:soil-water-295}}). Humans count explicitly as agents that change landscapes, and the field proposes ways to restore degraded ones.

soil-water-176.title: The van Genuchten model: a soil's water curve in a few numbers
soil-water-176.text: A whole {{ref:soil-water-175}} can be summed up in a few fitted numbers. The van Genuchten model is an equation that describes the shape of that curve. Its parameter α relates to the inverse of the air-entry suction, the suction at which air starts to enter the pores. The parameter n, always greater than 1, measures the pore-size distribution. Both come from field or laboratory tests, such as the instantaneous profile method, fitted by non-linear least squares. The parameterization led to a model predicting how a soil's conductivity when not saturated ({{ref:soil-phys-225}}) varies with saturation and pressure. Alternatives include the Brooks–Corey, Broadbridge–White and Rogers–Stallybrass–Clements models.

soil-water-229.title: Available water: the share of soil water plants can use
soil-water-229.text: Not all the water in a soil is water a plant can use. Available water capacity is the amount a soil profile can store and make available to growing crops. It is also called available water content (AWC), profile available water (PAW) or total available water (TAW). Frank Veihmeyer and Arthur Hendrickson defined readily available water as the difference between the water content at field capacity and at the permanent wilting point. This water sits in pores of 0.1–75 μm. Smaller cryptopores hold water too tightly for roots, and macropores are generally air-filled at field capacity. The definition is disputed. Daniel Hillel argued that its two limits were never clearly defined and lack a physical basis. Water, he said, is never equally available across the range. Richards, profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-023}}, called it oversimplified, since availability also depends on how readily soil water moves in to replace what roots take. Strongly alkaline, sodium-rich soils hold little, as do thin soils of the kind in {{ref:soil-class-050}}, while the fibrous clay of {{ref:soil-chem-167}} can raise plant-available water in sandy soils.

soil-water-290.title: Filter strips, grass that catches runoff
soil-water-290.text: A band of grass at a field's edge can catch what rain washes off the field. Such a band, described in {{ref:soil-agri-160}}, is a strip of grass or other permanent plants that shields streamside land from runoff carrying sediment, pest-killing chemicals, pathogens and nutrients. Strips work best when other conservation practices steer water toward them. Once mainly agricultural, they are now common in towns. They are not the same as a {{ref:soil-water-109}}. The mapping tool AgBufferBuilder designs them by mapping where uneven runoff flows.
